items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: The text describes Earl Tucker as an amateur who became famous at Connie's Inn, but the interviewee does not claim to have met, played with, or had a personal relationship with him; the mention is part of a general narrative about the venue's history.

ctx.x: The things those amateurs did was worth more than the admission fee to get into the Savoy to see. But there were other amateur acts, acrobats, contortionists and musicians.

One amateur who became famous especially in New York at Connie's Inn was a young fellow named Earl Tucker. He had come from Baltimore and wore sailor pants and shoes with tap dancers taps on them. He was a double-jointed fellow and could twist his body like a snake dancer and tap dance at the same time. He could stand back on his leg in a way that one would think they were going to break and he won the first prize the first time he came to Opportunity night. People started calling him "Snake Hips" and it was not…

The most fantastic personality to take part in these amateur contests was a violinist called Brother Brodie. Some people had asked me if I had ever seen or heard him. I hadn't so I asked for some information about him and all that they would tell me was wait.......
